Resolve field aliases before calling field_transformer

* Resolve field aliases before calling field_transformer

Previously, field_transformer received attributes with alias=None for
fields without an explicit alias. The default alias (e.g., stripping
leading underscores) was only resolved after the transformer ran, making
it impossible for transformers to access or use alias values.

This moves alias resolution to before the field_transformer call, so
transformers receive fully populated Attribute objects. A second pass
after the transformer handles any new fields the transformer may have
added.

Additionally, Attribute.evolve() now automatically updates the alias
when the name changes, if the alias was auto-generated (matching the
default for the old name). Explicit aliases are preserved.

Add `ne` validator

* Fix inconsistent formatting for Args and Raises docstrings

* Add `ne` validator

This change adds a validator that raises `ValueError` if the
initializer is called with a number equal to *val*.

An example use case. I want a field that is a signed `int` of any
value except for zero. I could do the following.

```python
attrs.field(
    validator=attrs.validators.or_(
        attrs.validators.le(-1),
        attrs.validators.ge(1),
    )
)
```

With this proposed `ne` validator I could do.

```python
attrs.field(validator=attrs.validators.ne(0))
```

perf(json): pooled-buffer JSON deserialize

* perf(json): reuse pooled buffer for JSON deserialization

DefaultJSONSerializer.Deserialize used json.NewDecoder(body).Decode(),
which allocates a decoder and its internal read buffer on every JSON
request. Read the body into a capped pooled buffer and decode with
json.Unmarshal instead; Unmarshal does not retain the input slice, so the
buffer is safe to reuse. The pool drops oversized buffers (>64 KiB) so a
large body cannot pin memory.

BenchmarkBind_JSON: 1008 B -> 312 B/op (-69%), 9 -> 7 allocs, ~12% faster.

Behavioral note: json.Unmarshal is stricter than Decode — it rejects
trailing data after the JSON value and reports "unexpected end of JSON
input" for truncated bodies (both still 400 Bad Request). Two bind tests
asserting the old "unexpected EOF" message are updated to match.

Also add a general ServeHTTP/JSON benchmark suite (perf_bench_test.go):
BenchmarkBind_JSON now builds the request once and resets a reusable body
instead of calling httptest.NewRequest inside the loop (which dominated
the old measurement), plus BenchmarkJSONSerialize/Deserialize and the
routing benchmarks used to measure both this and the companion router PR.


* test(json): cover pooled-buffer Deserialize behaviors

Add correctness coverage for the new pooled-buffer JSON deserializer,
addressing gaps surfaced in review:

- RejectsTrailingData: documents that json.Unmarshal rejects content after
  the first top-level value (a behavior change from streaming json.Decoder).
- PooledBufferReuse: long body followed by a short one must not leak stale
  bytes through the reused buffer.
- PooledBufferConcurrent: many goroutines decoding distinct bodies; under
  -race this catches any aliasing/missing-reset regression (data bleed).
- LargeBodyThenNormal: exercises the >64 KiB buffer-cap path and that the
  oversized buffer does not corrupt the next request.
- BodyReadError: a failing body read surfaces as 400, matching prior behavior.

feat: add support for HTTP QUERY method

Add first-class support for the QUERY HTTP method (RFC 10008) so it can
be registered with dedicated helpers instead of the generic `Add`.

QUERY is not (yet) part of the `net/http` standard library, so it is
defined in Echo the same way the existing non-standard PROPFIND and
REPORT methods are handled:

- add the `QUERY` method constant
- add `Echo.QUERY` and `Group.QUERY` route helpers
- give QUERY a dedicated field in `routeMethods` and wire it into
  `set`, `find`, `updateAllowHeader` and `isHandler`
- bind URL query parameters for QUERY (like GET/DELETE/HEAD), since
  QUERY is semantically a GET carrying its query in the body

fix(bind): honor OpenAPI date, date-time and date-time-local format tags

Swag and OpenAPI put format names such as `format:"date-time"` on `time.Time` fields. Echo treated those names as Go time layouts, so valid input failed to bind.

- `date-time` uses the same RFC3339 decoding as an untagged `time.Time`.
- `date-time-local` accepts `2006-01-02T15:04:05` with optional fractional seconds, rejects time-zone suffixes, and assigns UTC.
- `date` accepts `2006-01-02` and assigns UTC.
- Other `format` values are still Go layouts. Slice fields, JSON/XML decoding, and custom unmarshalers are unchanged.

fix(router): grow PathValues for contexts created before a route with more params

Adding a route with more path params after Echo has served requests panicked with "index out of range" on the next request that matched it, with both DefaultRouter and ConcurrentRouter. Pooled Contexts keep the PathValues capacity they were created with. DefaultRouter.Route detected the short capacity but allocated a zero-length slice and then set values by index.

The Context's PathValues are now grown at full length in that branch and kept, so later requests do not grow them again. The Router contract documents that Route must handle such Contexts.

fix(middleware): reject empty tokens in CSRF validation

subtle.ConstantTimeCompare treats two empty byte slices as equal, so
validateCSRFToken("", "") returns true. Extractors in extractor.go
treat a present-but-empty query/form/header value as successfully
extracted, so an attacker can supply an empty client token with no
special access. If the stored cookie token is ever empty (e.g. an
app clears it to "" instead of expiring it, or CookieSecure is false
and the cookie is overwritten over plain HTTP), CSRF validation is
bypassed entirely. Reject empty tokens before the comparison.

darwin: close select fallback fd

The Darwin select fallback keeps the original stream descriptor in
`s->fd` while the I/O watcher uses a socketpair. Stream cleanup joins
the selector thread and closes the socketpair, but did not close that
original descriptor.

win: don't fail fs event watch on locked files

uv_fs_event_start() opens the path with FILE_LIST_DIRECTORY to tell
files and directories apart. On a file that is FILE_READ_DATA, so the
open takes part in the sharing check and fails with
ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION when some other process has the file open
without FILE_SHARE_READ: a compiler emitting an object file, an
installer, a virus scanner. Up to 1.51.0 the type was determined with
GetFileAttributesW(), which never opened the path, so watching such a
file used to work.

Probe the type with FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES instead. It is all that
GetFileInformationByHandle() needs and it stays out of the sharing
check. Then open what is actually watched, the path itself when it is a
directory and its parent otherwise, and check the type of that handle
too.

Metadata still never comes from a path lookup, so the race fixed in
#4948 stays fixed, and the directory case gains the same post-open check
the file case already had.

The file branch still opens the parent by name and keeps its post-open
directory check; Win32 has no relative open short of NtCreateFile.

Reland "win: don't fail fs event watch on locked files"

This reverts commit 7a02ab5f400e6f0fdbf63253cc640df19c60f484, with fixes so that
ReOpenFile works as documented by calling the internal NtCreateFile operation
directly instead.

ReOpenFile() cannot reopen a directory handle: it unconditionally asks the
kernel for a non-directory file, so the underlying NtCreateFile() call fails
with STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY, which Windows' NTSTATUS-to- Win32 mapping
reports as the misleading ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED. This broke every directory watch
(uv_fs_event_start() on a directory), which is why CI failed across all Windows
configurations and the fix for #5272 had to be reverted.

Add uv__reopen_file(), a small wrapper around NtCreateFile() that reopens a
handle relative to itself (RootDirectory set to the handle, name left empty).
This achieves the same thing ReOpenFile() does for files, but also works for
directories, and keeps the original fix's goal of never resolving the path a
second time (so a concurrent rename cannot swap the watched directory out from
under us).

Verified on native Windows (cross-compiled with mingw, run via WSL2 interop)
that the previous revision reproduces the exact CI failure (`error: -4048`,
UV_EPERM from ReOpenFile()'s ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) on every directory-watching
fs_event test, and that this fix resolves all of them with no regressions
elsewhere in the suite.

I've asked Microsoft to fix `ReOpenFile`, but that would take a long time, if
they ever do: https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/sdk-api/pull/2262

idna: reject invalid continuation bytes

The continuation-byte check combines high bits with XOR, allowing
invalid bytes to cancel each other out. E2 41 42 is decoded as U+2042
and successfully converted to IDNA instead of being rejected.

Validate each continuation byte before decoding the code point while
preserving valid-input behavior and cursor advancement on errors.

Add decoder, IDNA and synchronous/asynchronous getaddrinfo regressions.

win: use a 64 KB buffer for recursive fs events

A recursive uv_fs_event_t reports changes for a whole tree through one
ReadDirectoryChangesW buffer, which libuv has always set at 4 KB. The system
discards everything in it when it overflows, and the callback gets a NULL
filename.

This is easy to hit. libuv only issues the next read once the callbacks for the
previous batch have returned, so the loop is often busy with the consumer's
response to earlier changes, and about 13 file writes arriving in that window
are enough to overflow it. Installing a package into node_modules overflows
more often than not.

Give recursive handles 64 KB instead. Each change is a 12-byte record plus its
relative path in UTF-16, so creating and writing a file with a 50-character
path costs about 310 bytes, and 64 KB holds about 210 such files. 64 KB is also
the largest size that works on network shares: larger sizes are accepted by the
call, but the read then fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER.

Non-recursive watches keep 4 KB. The system matches each handle's buffer with
its own buffer of the same size, and programs that watch directories one at a
time can hold thousands of handles. Flat watches also have shorter relative
paths, and an overflow there costs a single directory listing to recover from.

The system keeps the buffer size and the recursive setting from the first call
on a handle, so every call has to pass the same size. Store the recursive bit
in a new flag. This also fixes the re-arm, which tested UV_FS_EVENT_RECURSIVE
against the handle flags, where that bit is UV_HANDLE_ACTIVE, and so always
asked for a recursive watch. That was harmless because the system ignores the
change.

darwin: add LaunchServices process title opt-out

Allow applications to skip LaunchServices registration and display name
updates by setting UV_PROCESS_TITLE_USE_LAUNCH_SERVICES=0 at startup
Keep the default enabled to preserve Activity Monitor behavior.

Capture the setting in uv_setup_args so concurrent title updates do not
read the environment, and retain argv updates and thread naming when
LaunchServices is disabled.

Add regression coverage for value parsing, repeated updates and setting
changes after initialization, and document the opt-out.
